title: Transpose, Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices
quickIdea: Transposing reflects a matrix in its main diagonal and reverses products; symmetric means A^T = A, skew-symmetric means A^T = -A, and every square matrix splits uniquely into one of each.
remember: (A^T)_ij = a_ji; (A^T)^T = A; (A + B)^T = A^T + B^T; (kA)^T = kA^T; (AB)^T = B^T A^T; (A^-1)^T = (A^T)^-1.
Symmetric: A^T = A. Skew-symmetric: A^T = -A, which forces every diagonal entry to be 0 and forces a_ij = -a_ji off the diagonal.
Every square matrix splits uniquely as A = (A + A^T)/2 + (A - A^T)/2, a symmetric part plus a skew-symmetric part.
A^T A and A A^T are always symmetric, even when A is rectangular.
A skew-symmetric matrix of odd order has determinant 0, so it is singular; of even order it can be non-singular, for example [[0,1],[-1,0]].
The rank of a skew-symmetric matrix is never 1: it is 0 or at least 2.

example.prompt: A = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]. Compute A^T A and explain why it must be symmetric.
example.work: A^T is 3 x 2, so A^T A is 3 x 3 with (A^T A)_ij equal to column i of A dotted with column j of A: 17, 22, 27 on the first row; 22, 29, 36 on the second; 27, 36, 45 on the third.
example.answer: A^T A = [[17,22,27],[22,29,36],[27,36,45]], symmetric because a dot product does not care about the order of its two factors.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.37 asks which properties survive swapping two rows of a square matrix: the determinant changes sign and invertibility survives, but symmetry and the trace do not.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: How many 3 x 3 symmetric matrices are there with every entry 0 or 1?
variations.why: The three diagonal entries and the three entries above the diagonal are free, and the entries below the diagonal are then forced, so the count is 2^(3 x 4 / 2).

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why must a skew-symmetric matrix of odd order be singular?
variations.answer: Because det(A) = det(A^T) = det(-A) = (-1)^n det(A), and for odd n that reads det(A) = -det(A), so det(A) = 0.
variations.why: The three steps are the transpose law, the definition of skew-symmetric, and the scalar law det(kA) = k^n det(A) with k = -1.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A and B are symmetric matrices of the same order. When is AB symmetric?
variations.why: (AB)^T = B^T A^T = BA, so AB equals its own transpose if and only if AB = BA.

trap.why: The order of the factors reverses. The wrong version agrees with the right one only when AB = BA.
trap.counterexample: A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,0],[1,0]]: AB = [[1,0],[0,0]] is already symmetric, but A^T B^T = [[0,0],[0,1]], which is a different matrix.

check.question: A is 3 x 3 and skew-symmetric. What is det(A)?
check.explanation: For odd order, det(A) = det(A^T) = det(-A) = (-1)^3 det(A) = -det(A), so det(A) = 0; a 3 x 3 skew-symmetric matrix is always singular.
